column2: His great eyes red with rage, the mighty-armed Shalya, proud of his family, sovereignty, learning and strength, turned about and said this:

You slight me, son of Gandhari, or you surely suspect me, since you say to me confidently, 'Be a charioteer.'
mahabharata:8:23.22	Considering Karna superior to us, you praise him; but I do not reckon Radheya in battle as equal to myself.
mahabharata:8:23.23	Assign me a greater share, O lord of the earth; having slain him in battle I shall go as I came.
mahabharata:8:23.24	Or I shall fight alone, delight of the Kurus; see my prowess today in battle as I burn my foes.
mahabharata:8:23.25	A man like me, O Kaurava, does not act merely to satisfy others' wishes; do not be too suspicious of me.
mahabharata:8:23.26	In battle no insult is ever to be offered me. See these two arms of mine, like thunderbolts.
mahabharata:8:23.27	See my variegated bow, my arrows like venomous serpents, my chariot with fine horses swift as the wind, and my mace adorned with gold plates, son of Gandhari.
mahabharata:8:23.28	In rage I could split the earth, scatter the mountains and dry up the seas with my own splendour, O king.
mahabharata:8:23.29	Knowing me to be so, capable of subduing foes, why do you engage me as charioteer of Adhiratha's lesser son?
mahabharata:8:23.30	You ought not, O king of kings, to yoke me to the pole. I do not dare to be a servant when I am better than a worse man.
mahabharata:8:23.31	He who, having come with affection, places a greater man under a lesser one, commits a sin that turns things upside down.
mahabharata:8:23.32	Brahmanas were created by Brahma from his mouth, kshatriyas from his chest, vaishyas from his thighs, shudras from his feet—so the scripture says; from them arose the special castes, born of reversed and direct unions.
mahabharata:8:23.33	Then, by the intermingling of one another, in the four orders, O Bharata, kshatriyas are held to be protectors, receivers and givers.
mahabharata:8:23.34	Brahmanas were established on earth by Brahma for the good of the world with sacrificing, teaching and pure acceptance of gifts.
mahabharata:8:23.35	Agriculture, cattle-keeping and giving belong in every way to vaishyas; shudras are appointed as servants of Brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaishyas.
mahabharata:8:23.36	Sutas are appointed as servants of Brahmana and kshatriya, not of vaishya and shudra; hear my word on this, sinless one.
mahabharata:8:23.37	I, consecrated on the head, born in a family of royal sages, am known as a great chariot-warrior, to be served and praised by bards.
mahabharata:8:23.38	Being such, O crusher of enemy families, I will not act as charioteer in battle to the son of a charioteer.
mahabharata:8:23.39	Having met with disrespect I shall not fight at all; taking leave of you today, son of Gandhari, I shall go as I came.
Having said this, the tiger among men, Shalya, ornament of assemblies, rose and quickly left the midst of the kings, indignant.
Your son, with affection and great regard, held him back and spoke sweet, conciliatory words that accomplish everything.

As you say, Shalya, so it surely is, without doubt; but I have a certain intention; understand it, lord of men.
mahabharata:8:23.43	I do not at all suspect that Karna is superior to you; the lord of the Madras would never do what is untrue.
mahabharata:8:23.44	Your ancestors, best of men, bore only truth; therefore I think you are called Artayani.
mahabharata:8:23.45	Because you are a thorn (shalya) to your enemies on earth, O giver of honour, you are called Shalya, O lord of the earth.
mahabharata:8:23.46	What you said earlier, giver of rich gifts, do that very thing, knower of dharma, whatever I tell you for my sake.
mahabharata:8:23.47	Neither Radheya is greater than you nor am I more valiant; we choose you as driver of the best horses in battle.
mahabharata:8:23.48	As the world thinks Karna superior in qualities to Dhananjaya and even to Vasudeva, so it thinks of you.
mahabharata:8:23.49	Karna is superior to Partha in weapons, O bull among men, and you are superior to Krishna in horse-driving and strength.
mahabharata:8:23.50	As the great-minded Vasudeva knows the heart of horses, you know it twice as well, king of the Madras; there is no doubt.
[Shalya said:] "Son of Gandhari, since you say in the midst of the army that I am superior to Devaki's son, I am pleased with you.
I take on the charioteering of the renowned Radheya as he fights the foremost of the Pandavas, as you, hero, desire.
But there is a condition of mine, hero, with regard to Vaikartana: in his presence I may speak freely as I wish."
[Sanjaya said:] "So be it," O king, said your son with Karna to the Madra king's son, O best of the Bharatas.
[Duryodhana said:] "What the great sage Markandeya told my father, hear in full as I tell it, best of royal sages; you need make no further inquiry.
There was a great encounter between gods and asuras; the first battle, O king, was the Taraka war, and, as we have heard, the daityas were then conquered by the gods.
When the daityas were conquered, the three sons of Taraka—Tarakaksha, Kamalaksha and Vidyunmalin, O king—
taking up fierce austerity and abiding in the highest observances, wasted their own bodies with penance, scorcher of foes.
With self-control, austerity and observance, O king, the Grandsire was pleased and, giver of boons, granted them boons.
Together they chose from the Grandsire of all the worlds immunity from death, O king, from all beings always.
The god, lord and master of the worlds, said to them: "There is no immortality for all; desist from this, asuras; choose another boon, whatever pleases you."
Then, O king, they together deliberated many times, bowed to the lord of all the worlds and said:

Grant us this boon, O god, Grandsire: that, resorting to three cities, we may roam this earth in this world, honoured by your grace.
mahabharata:8:24.11	After a thousand years we shall meet each other, and these cities, sinless one, will become one.
mahabharata:8:24.12	And when these have joined, whoever, O Lord, best of gods, shall destroy them with a single arrow shall be our death. Saying "So be it" to them, the god returned to heaven.
Having obtained their boon, they were pleased and, after deliberating together, chose the great asura Maya, ageless Vishvakarma, honoured by daityas and danavas, to build the three cities.
Then the wise Maya by his own austerity made three cities: one of gold, one of silver and one of black iron.
The golden one was in heaven, the silver in the sky, and the iron one on earth, resting on a wheel, O lord of the earth.
Each measured a hundred yojanas in breadth and length, with houses, towers and turrets, a great rampart and gateways,
crowded with every excellence yet uncrowded, free from disease, adorned with palaces of many kinds and with gates.
In the cities, O king, there were separate kings: the wondrous golden one belonged to the great-souled Tarakaksha, the silver one to Kamalaksha and the iron one to Vidyunmalin.
Those three daitya kings, by their splendour, quickly overran the three worlds and remained for multitudes of years, as the Lord of Creatures ordained.
Of those chief danavas, tens of thousands, hundreds of millions and crores of unmatched heroes gathered from every side, desiring great sovereignty, relying on the fortress of Tripura.
For all of them Maya bore the burden of every device, and relying on him they all lived free of fear.
Whatever desire anyone in Tripura conceived in mind, Maya then by his magic fulfilled each one.
There was a mighty son of Tarakaksha named Hari, who practised supreme austerity, by which the Grandsire was pleased.
Pleased, he chose of the god: "Let there be a pool in our city, in which those slain by weapons and cast in will become stronger."
Having obtained the boon, the hero Hari, son of Tarakaksha, created there that pool, O lord, restoring the dead to life.
In whatever form and dress a daitya died and was cast into it, he came to life in just that same form.
Having obtained it, those dwelling in Tripura oppressed all the worlds, perfected by great austerity, increasing the gods' fear; they suffered no destruction in battle at all, O king.
Then, overcome by greed and delusion, senseless, shameless, they all plundered the established order.
Having driven the gods with their hosts from place to place at every turn, they roamed, proud of their desire and their boon.

Those wicked-conducted danavas, transgressing all limits, destroyed all the forests of the gods, the dear places of the dwellers in heaven, the holy hermitages of sages, sacrificial posts and settlements.
All those gods together, O tamer of foes, then went to the Grandsire to tell him of the injury done by the foes of the gods.
Telling him the whole truth and bowing with their heads, they asked the Lord Grandsire for a means of slaying them.
Hearing it, the Lord God said to the gods: "Those evil-souled asuras, and also those, O wise ones, who hate the gods, constantly offend, they who oppress you.
I am the same to all beings, no doubt; but I tell you that the unrighteous must be slain.
You, Adityas, choose Sthanu, Ishana, the victorious, of effortless action, as fighter; he will slay those enemies of the gods."
Hearing his words, the gods led by Shakra, with Brahma before them, went to take refuge with the bull-bannered one (Shiva).
They practised supreme austerity, chanting the eternal Brahman, and with the sages, knowers of dharma, took refuge in Bhava with all their being.
They praised with meaningful words the greatest giver of fearlessness in dangers, the Self of all, the great soul by whom all is pervaded by the self,
who by many special austerities knows the yoga of the Self, who knows the Sankhya of the Self, and whose Self is always self-controlled.
They saw that Ishana, a mass of splendour, lord of Uma, unequalled in the world, observant of vows and sinless.
They imagined that one Lord in many forms; in the great soul they saw forms corresponding to their own, and saw each other, all greatly astonished.
The gods and Brahmin sages bowed their heads to the earth before that unborn lord of the world, who is made of all beings.
Shankara, honouring them with blessings and raising them up, the Lord said smiling, "Speak, speak."
Permitted by the three-eyed one, their minds at ease, they said to Bhava, "Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord."

Salutations to the god of gods, the bowman, of great wrath, destroyer of the sacrifice of the Lord of Creatures, praised by the Lords of Creatures.
mahabharata:8:24.46	Salutations to him who is praised, to be praised, being praised, to Death; to the red one, Rudra, the blue-necked, the bearer of the trident.
mahabharata:8:24.47	To the unerring, the deer-eyed, the fighter with the best weapons, the hard to restrain, the pure, the Brahman, the celibate student.
mahabharata:8:24.48	To Ishana, the immeasurable, the controller, the one clad in hide, the ever-austere, the tawny, the vow-keeper, the one clad in skin.
mahabharata:8:24.49	To the father of Kumara, the three-eyed, the bearer of the best weapons, the destroyer of the distress of those who seek refuge, the slayer of hosts that hate Brahman.
mahabharata:8:24.50	Salutations to the lord of trees, lord of men, always lord of cattle, lord of sacrifices.
mahabharata:8:24.51	Salutations to you with your host, to the three-eyed, of fierce splendour; with mind, speech and deeds, O God, cherish us who have taken refuge in you.
Then the pleased Lord, welcoming them with a greeting, said: "Let your fear depart; say what I shall do for you."
When the great soul had granted the boon to the hosts of fathers, gods and sages, Brahma, honouring Shankara, spoke words for the good of the world.

By your creation, Lord of the gods, this office of Prajapati exists; I, occupying it, gave the danavas a great boon.
mahabharata:8:24.55	None other than you can destroy those who have transgressed limits, O lord of past and future; you are their opponent in slaying.
mahabharata:8:24.56	So, O God, show favour to the gods who beg you, who have taken refuge; slay the danavas, trident-bearer.
[The Lord said:] "My view is that all your enemies must be slain; but I alone am not able to kill those enemies of the gods.
All of you together, with the splendour of my weapon, conquer those foes in battle, for the host is very strong."
[The gods said:] "As much as our splendour and strength is, they have twice as much, we think, for we have seen their splendour and strength."
[The Lord said:] "Those sinners who offend against you are to be slain by all; with half my splendour and strength, slay all those foes."
[The gods said:] "We shall not be able to bear half your splendour, Maheshvara; slay the foes yourself with half the strength of all of us."
[Duryodhana said:] "Then, saying 'So be it,' the lord of the gods, addressed by them, O best of kings, took half of everything and became greater in splendour than all.
That god was stronger in strength than all, and from then Shankara was known as Mahadeva.
Then Mahadeva said: "I who bear bow and arrow shall slay those foes, O dwellers in heaven, in battle from a chariot.
You, see for me a chariot, bow and arrow, while today I fell them on the ground."
[The gods said:] "Taking the essence of the whole form of the three worlds from here and there, we shall prepare for you a chariot of great splendour, lord of the gods."
Thus the beautiful chariot was made by Vishvakarma, devised by intellect; then those tigers among the gods prepared that chariot.
They made the earth goddess, with her broad cities like garlands, with mountains, forests and islands, the bearer of beings, as the chariot's seat.
Mount Mandara was the axle, great rivers its legs, the quarters and intermediate quarters the retinue of the chariot.
Bright planets were the draught-poles, the stars the covering, the three-fold pole joined with dharma, artha and kama was the seat, and there were many herbs with many flowers and fruits.
Having made the sun and moon the two wheels of that best of chariots, they made the two wings, east and west, and day and night were made fair.
The ten lords of snakes led by Dhritarashtra were its shaft, heaven the yoke, with yoke-skins and the clouds of destruction.
Shami, Dhriti, Medha, Sthiti and Sannati, with the planets, constellations and stars, made the variegated skin of the sky.
The lords of the world—gods, waters, the dead and wealth—were the horses; Sinivali, Anumati, Kuhu and Raka of good vows were the traces, and the two rising ones and the thorn.
Karma, truth, austerity and wealth were its reins; the mind was the seat, and Sarasvati the highway.
Banners of many colours, variegated, stirred by the wind, lit up the blazing chariot bound with lightning and the rainbow.
Thus, O great king, when that best of chariots was made by the gods, tiger among men, for crushing the foes,
Shankara placed on the chariot his chief weapons; he set the chariot's pole, drawn from the sky, with the bull.
The rod of Brahma, the rod of Time, the rod of Rudra and fever were the chariot's supports, raised on every side.
The Atharva and Angirasa were the great soul's wheel-guards, with the Rigveda, Samaveda and Purana before them.
History and the Yajurveda were the rear guards; divine speech and the sciences were made side-attendants.
Goads and so on, O king of kings, and the vashat call, and the syllable Om at the front, were its great ornament.
Making the year the many-coloured bow with the six seasons, they made the string from the ageless Night of Time, bane of men.
Vishnu became the arrow, with Fire and Soma; Agni and Soma are the whole world, and the world is called Vaishnava.
Vishnu is the self of the Lord Bhava of immeasurable splendour; therefore they could not bear the touch of Hara's bowstring.
On that arrow the Lord of fierce anger loosed the unbearable fire of wrath born of the anger of Bhrigu and Angiras.
That blue-and-red, smoky, hide-clad, dreadful one, like ten thousand suns, blazing wrapped in flames of splendour,
hard to dislodge, dislodging, victor, slayer of those who hate Brahman, Hara, always saviour and slayer of men devoted to dharma and adharma,
surrounded by crushing, dreadful, terrible and towering hosts, the Lord Sthanu shone, surrounded by those very qualities of his own self.
The whole world, moving and unmoving, resting on his limbs, shone, O king, wondrous to behold.
Seeing that divine chariot, armoured and with bow, he took that divine arrow born of Soma, Vishnu and Agni.
Then the gods made the Lord's horses, O king: the wind bearing pure fragrance.
Mounting it, Mahadeva, terrifying even the gods, climbed up then, alert, as if making heaven and earth tremble.
Shining, the boon-giver, with sword, arrows and bow, the god said, laughing, "Who will be my charioteer?"
The hosts of gods said to him, "Whomever you appoint, Lord of the gods, he will be your charioteer, no doubt."
The god said to them again, "Whoever is superior to me, make him my charioteer, reflecting yourselves, without delay."
Hearing the words spoken by the great soul, the gods went to the god Grandsire, propitiated him and spoke thus:

O God, you have told us of the destroyer of the gods' foes, and so we have done; the bull-bannered one is pleased.
mahabharata:8:24.99	A chariot has been made by us, equipped with marvellous weapons, but we do not know who should be the charioteer on that best of chariots.
mahabharata:8:24.100	Therefore let some charioteer be appointed, best of gods; you ought to make that word of yours fruitful for us, O Lord.
mahabharata:8:24.101	For earlier, Lord, you told us, 'I shall do good to you'; you ought to do that.
mahabharata:8:24.102	This best of chariots of ours, O God, is difficult to resist and routs the foes; Pinaka-handed is the fighter placed here, who, rising, terrifies the danavas.
mahabharata:8:24.103	So too the four Vedas are the best horses, the earth with her mountains is the chariot of the great soul, the lineage of stars follows in the covering; the charioteer must protect the warrior in it.
mahabharata:8:24.104	In it a charioteer must be sought, one distinguished by all these; the chariot, the horses and likewise the fighter rest on him, and the armour, weapons and bow, Grandsire.
mahabharata:8:24.105	Other than you we see no other charioteer there; you are endowed with all qualities and superior to the gods, Lord. Quickly mount in the charioteer's place and rein in the best horses.
Thus, bowing their heads to the Grandsire, lord of the three worlds, the gods propitiated him to be charioteer, as we have heard.
[Brahma said:] "There is nothing false in what you have said, O dwellers in heaven; I shall rein in the horses for the matted-haired one as he fights."
Then that Lord God, creator of worlds, the Grandsire, was appointed by the gods as charioteer of the great-souled Ishana.
When he quickly mounted that chariot honoured by the world, the wind-swift horses at once bowed their heads to the ground.
When Maheshvara mounted, they went down on their knees to the earth.
The great-grandsire, lord of the three worlds, gathering the reins, urged those horses swift as thought and wind.
Then, when the boon-giver had mounted and set out against the asuras, the lord of all, smiling, said, "Well done, well done!"
Go, god, to where the daityas are; drive the horses unwearied. See today the strength of my arms as I slay my foes in battle.
Then he drove those wind-swift horses to where the Tripura was, O king, guarded by daityas and danavas.
Then Sharva strung his bow, fixed that arrow, united it with the Pashupata weapon and meditated on Tripura.
While he stood thus, enraged, with his bow drawn, those cities in time came into union.
When the cities had come together as one, a tumultuous joy arose among the great-souled gods.
Then all hosts of gods, siddhas and great sages uttered cries of "Victory!" praising him, full of joy.
Then the Tripura, while slaying the asuras, appeared before him, of fearful form and unbearable splendour of the god.
Drawing back that divine bow, the Lord of the worlds loosed the arrow, the essence of the three worlds, at Tripura; it burnt it with its band of asuras and cast it into the western sea.
Thus Tripura and all the danavas were burnt without remainder by Maheshvara, enraged, wishing well to the three worlds.
And the fire born of his own wrath, crying "Alas," was restrained; the three-eyed one said to it, "Do not reduce the worlds to ashes."
Then the gods, worlds and sages, restored to their natural state, praised with meaningful words Sthanu of incomparable splendour.
Permitted by the Lord, they all went as they had come, with their desires fulfilled, the gods led by Prajapati, with him pleased.
As the Lord Brahma, upholder of the worlds and grandsire, held the reins, so you rein in the horses of this great-souled Radheya.
For you, especially, are superior to Krishna, to Karna and to Phalguna, tiger among kings; there is no doubt about it.
In battle this man is like Rudra, and you, sinless one, are equal to Brahma; therefore you two are able to conquer my enemies as those two the asuras.
As today, Shalya, this Karna may crush and slay the son of Kunti, white-horsed with Krishna as charioteer, arrange that swiftly; Karna, the kingdom and ourselves are all founded on you.
Hear from me another history that a Brahmana, knower of dharma, told in my father's presence.
Hearing this wondrous account with its reasons, causes and purposes, Shalya, decide and do it; let there be no hesitation here.
Born in the family of the Bhargavas was Jamadagni of great austerity; his son, renowned as Rama, was endowed with splendour and virtues.
Taking up intense austerity, he propitiated Bhava for the sake of weapons, with a calm mind, disciplined and with senses restrained.
Mahadeva was pleased with him for his devotion and tranquillity, and, knowing what was in his heart, Shankara showed himself.
[Ishvara said:] "Rama, I am pleased; may it be well with you. I know your desire. Make yourself pure and you shall obtain all this.
I shall give you weapons when you become pure; weapons burn the unworthy and the incapable, Bhargava."
Thus addressed by the god of gods, the trident-bearer, Jamadagni's son bowed his head and replied to the great lord:
Then a most tumultuous battle took place between the Kuru and Pandava armies, O best of the Bharatas, like the war of gods and asuras.
Fate cannot be transgressed by men, Gavalgani, since my son was felled in battle by meeting the Parthas.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing those pitiable words, tormented by the slaying of sons and grandsons, the unassailable one fell to the ground like a tree struck by the wind.
Narada, in due time, after reflecting with the sages, said to the righteous Yudhishthira words suited to the time.
On this point they cite this ancient history, the conversation of Death, Gautami, the hunter, time and the serpent.
I and Gandhari must grieve, lord of men, bereft of sons and kingdom, like one who has gained wealth in a dream.
Yudhishthira, O great king, presented to Dhritarashtra costly couches, garments, ornaments, all things fit for a king, and many kinds of food and drink.
[Janamejaya said:] "By whom were those heroes cursed, that the Vrishnis and Andhakas met destruction, and the Bhojas? Tell me in detail, best of the twice-born."
When Yadava Vajra, king at Shakra's city, and Parikshit at Hastinapura, they are to be protected by you; do not set your mind on unrighteousness.
And Draupadi, Panchali, devoted to dharma, of faultless limbs, our wife, was tormented in the midst of the assembly in the presence of the elders.
